title: Shooting Stars From Halley's Comet
summary:
Halley's Comet is far away — more than 3 billion miles (4.8 billion kilometers) from Earth. But tiny pieces it left behind still light up our sky.

On October 21, photographer Tim McCollum captured three bright Orionid meteors above Toccoa, Georgia. The Orionid meteor shower happens each autumn, when Earth passes through dust and debris shed by Halley's Comet. The tiny pieces burn up in our air and become shooting stars.

McCollum took photos between 3 and 4 a.m. He used a Canon camera on a star tracker and took many 30-second pictures. Then he combined them into one image.

His picture also shows Orion's Belt, the Orion Nebula and the Rosette Nebula, with the Milky Way cutting across the sky.

The Orionid shower stays active until November 7. On clear nights, you may still spot one of Halley's shooting stars.
why_it_matters: On a clear night, kids can look up and watch tiny pieces left by a faraway comet streak across the sky.
